narratives.narrative: The inner being here reckons with its own dignity. Contemplating 'what is man,' the interior registers that mankind has been GIVEN DOMINION (sense 101, mashal) over the works of God's hands. This is read as a state (102), not a self-initiated act - and fittingly the source (103) goes unrecorded: dominion is conferred, not self-generated; it arrives from outside as gift. No seat (104: none) lodges it in an organ - it is a standing of the whole person, whose locus is internal:ib-state (116). The bearer is mankind (105); the operation (106) is the human vocation contemplated - the crowned creature is also a ruler, responsibility folded into the honour - with target vocation itself (107), coupled as given-dominion (112). Manner (108: none) leaves uncoloured how it is held; intensity, specifier and effect are all silent (109/110/111), the psalm dwelling on the fact of the charge rather than its degree or its outworking. No prohibition (113). The finding is a characteristic (115): dominion as an inner reckoning with a calling.
narratives.story: Looking up at the vast sky, the psalmist asks why God would bother with a creature as small as a human being. The surprising answer is that people have been handed real authority over the world and everything in it. This was not earned or seized; it was simply given, placed in human hands from above. It is not a passing feeling but a settled standing that belongs to the whole person. And with the honour comes a task: to be crowned is also to be made a ruler, answerable for the world entrusted to us.

narratives.narrative: Here the inner being appears as the fixed character of the enemy: avlah, INJUSTICE / unrighteousness (sense 101), read as a status (102) rather than an action - a condition of the man, not a deed caught in motion. Accordingly operation (106: none), target (107: none) and manner (108: none) are all explicitly empty: the passage does not show this injustice doing anything in the moment; it names what the man is. Source (103) is unrecorded - no origin is given for the perversity; it simply constitutes him. No seat (104: none) locates it in an organ; it pervades the person (locus internal:ib-state, 116). The bearer is the unjust man (105) from whom the psalmist begs deliverance, and the single coupling pairs him with the deceitful man (112) - injustice keeping company with deceit, the two-fold portrait of the 'ungodly people.' Intensity, specifier, effect and prohibition are all silent (109-113): the reading refuses to embellish, registering a character rather than its measure. A characteristic (115).
narratives.story: The psalmist pleads to be rescued from a man he calls unjust. What stands out is that this injustice is not described as a single wrong the man commits, but as the kind of person he simply is - a crookedness woven through his whole character. The passage does not say where it came from or what it is doing at that exact moment; it just names it. And it never travels alone: the unjust man is paired with a deceitful one, so that dishonesty and injustice form a single portrait of the enemy the psalmist wants to escape.

narratives.narrative: This reading opens the interior of the enemy - and refuses to soften it. The assembled kings (bearer 105) are ASTOUNDED (sense 101, tamah), an action (102) of the mind stunned. Uniquely in this family a source (103) is named: God's terrifying power that shatters (v7), so the collapse is not self-caused but triggered from outside - the interior seized by what it beholds. The operation (106) is simply to be astounded, its target the sight of Zion (107); no seat (104: none) confines it to an organ (locus internal:ib-state, 116). Manner is unrecorded (108: none), yet the coupling (112) pairs the amazement with panic - the first move of a terror-sequence (astounded, panic, trembling, anguish) the discovery (114) traces. Intensity, specifier and effect are silent (109-111): the text names the shock without grading it. No prohibition (113). A characteristic (115): the foe's inner overthrow read with the same weight as any believer's wonder - dread that begins in the eyes and ends in flight.
narratives.story: Enemy kings gather and march against God's city, confident. But the moment they see it, something breaks inside them. They are stunned - not by anything they did to themselves, but by a power greater than they can face, the same power that will soon shatter their ships. The shock does not stay still: amazement tips into panic, panic into trembling, and trembling drives them to flee. The passage looks straight into the fear of God's foes and reports it plainly - dread that starts in the eyes and empties out into headlong flight.

narratives.narrative: The inner being here is the crowd's endorsement of folly. The people who follow (bearer 105) APPROVE (sense 101, ratsah - be pleased with), an action (102) directed at their boasts (target 107) - the vaunting of the doomed rich. Source (103) is unrecorded: no cause is named for the approval; it simply perpetuates itself down the generations. No seat (104: none) fixes it in an organ (locus internal:ib-state, 116); manner (108: none) is uncoloured. The coupling (112) marks the approvers as belonging to the foolishly confident - the endorsement binds the crowd to the folly it admires. Intensity, specifier and effect are silent (109-111): the psalm registers the approval without measuring how strong or with what result, though the surrounding verses supply the irony - those approved perish like beasts. No prohibition (113). Note the range of ratsah across this family (contrast H7521:pleas, consenting to a thief; H7521:hold, cherishing Zion's stones): here the same faculty of glad approval is bent onto boasting. A characteristic (115).
narratives.story: A rich man boasts of his wealth and lives as though he will never die. He does not; he perishes like an animal. Yet the striking thing is what the watching crowd does: they applaud. Generation after generation admires the very boasting that leads to the grave, endorsing the folly instead of seeing through it. The passage does not say why people do this or how deeply they feel it - only that this approval keeps the folly alive, and that the same capacity to admire could just as easily be turned toward what actually lasts.

narratives.narrative: This reading turns on an impossibility. The sense (101) is padah, to RANSOM / redeem - but negated: no man can. It is an action (102) whose bearer is 'no man' (105), able to do nothing; the operation (106) is ransom, explicitly negated, its target another - a brother (107). The manner (108) is emphatic, carried by the opening 'truly.' Crucially the prohibition dimension is present and marked negated (113): 'NO man can ransom another' - the passage's force lies in what cannot be done. Source (103) is unrecorded, and coupling is none (112) - the impotence stands alone, unattached. No seat (104: none) locates it (locus internal:ib-state, 116); intensity, specifier and effect are silent (109-111). The discovery (114) names the point: wealth is powerless before death; no human price buys off the grave, the great equaliser the rich forget. A characteristic (115): a truth the interior must reckon with - the limit that levels pomp.
narratives.story: The psalm confronts a hard fact about money and death. No matter how rich a person is, he cannot buy back his own life or anyone else's; there is no price high enough to pay off the grave. The word 'truly' underlines it - this is stated as flat, unarguable reality. What matters here is precisely what cannot be done: the wealthy imagine their riches make them safe, but death takes rich and poor alike. The passage lets that impossibility stand on its own, a leveling truth that strips away every boast.

narratives.narrative: The inner being here is exposed through the company it keeps. The sense (101) is naaph, ADULTERERS / to commit adultery, an action (102) whose bearer is the adulterers themselves - the wicked's chosen company (105). The operation (106) is to commit adultery, but the target (107: none) is left empty: the reading does not fix an object; the point is not a particular act but a shared condition. Source (103) is unrecorded; no seat (104: none) locates it (locus internal:ib-state, 116); manner (108: none) is uncoloured. The one coupling (112) names the mechanism: this is the company the wicked keeps - fellowship with the immoral. Intensity, specifier and effect are silent (109-111). No prohibition (113), though the whole indictment is God's charge against the wicked who mouth his covenant while consorting with thieves and adulterers. The discovery (114) calls it corruption by association. A characteristic (115): the interior known by whom it runs with.
narratives.story: God turns to accuse the wicked man who recites his laws while living against them. One charge is the crowd he chooses: he delights in thieves and keeps easy company with adulterers. The point is not a single act pinned to a single moment, but the kind of people he is at home among - the immoral are his fellowship. A person is revealed by the company he keeps, and this man has thrown in his lot with the unfaithful. His corruption spreads by association, caught from those he chooses to stand beside.

narratives.narrative: Distinct from the adulterers he keeps company with, this reading isolates the inward consent itself. The sense (101) is ratsah - to be PLEASED with, to consent - an action (102) whose bearer is the wicked (105) and whose target is the thief (107). The operation (106) is to be pleased / consent: seeing a thief, the heart approves. Source (103) is unrecorded; no seat (104: none) fixes it (locus internal:ib-state, 116); manner (108: none) is uncoloured. The coupling (112) pairs this consent with keeping company with adulterers - the two verses of the indictment holding together, inward approval and outward fellowship. Intensity, specifier and effect are silent (109-111); no prohibition (113). The discovery (114) names it inner complicity with evil, and marks the irony against ratsah's proper use (approving God's ways). Preserving the distinction from H5003:adulterer in the same verse: adultery names the company, this names the heart that consents to it. A characteristic (115).
narratives.story: The same accusation against the wicked man reaches deeper here. When he sees a thief at work, he is glad - his heart takes the thief's side. This is the inner approval underneath the outward friendships: first the heart consents to the wrong, then the company follows. The word for being pleased is the very one used for delighting in God's ways, which makes the twist sharper - the same power of approval that should welcome good is here bent toward theft and betrayal. It is complicity from the inside out.

narratives.narrative: In the great penitential prayer the inner being is asked for a specific disposition. The sense (101) is nadib - WILLING, free, noble, the root of freewill offerings - read as a status (102), a condition of the self rather than a single act. Uniquely here a seat (104) is named: the spirit; and the locus (116) is internal:spirit, the deepest register of the person. The bearer is the penitent (105); the operation (106) is to be upheld by it - the willing spirit sustains him - with target none (107), since it is not aimed outward but holds him steady. Source (103) is unrecorded: the disposition is asked of God ('uphold me'), not self-produced. Manner (108: none) is uncoloured. The coupling (112) pairs it with the restored joy of salvation - readiness and joy together as the fruit of pardon. Intensity, specifier and effect are silent (109-111); no prohibition (113). The discovery (114) names it a free, generous, glad obedience, second of the psalm's three spirit-states. A characteristic (115).
narratives.story: In his prayer for forgiveness, David asks not just to be cleansed but to be changed inside. He begs for a willing spirit - an eager, generous, ready readiness to obey, the opposite of grudging duty. This is not a passing mood but a settled state seated in the very spirit of a person, and he cannot manufacture it himself; he asks God to uphold him with it. It comes bound together with restored joy: the forgiven heart is both glad and glad to obey. What he wants is an inner disposition that gladly says yes.

narratives.narrative: This reads the interior of the godless as a settled ruin. The sense (101) is shachat - to be CORRUPT, act ruinously, spoil - a status (102), a condition following the fool's denial of God 'in his heart.' The bearer is the fools / mankind (105); the operation (106) is to be corrupt / act ruinously, but target (107: none) is empty - corruption here is not aimed at an object; it is what they have become. Source (103) is unrecorded, though the passage's logic supplies it (the heart that says 'no God'); no seat (104: none) fixes it (locus internal:ib-state, 116); manner (108: none) is uncoloured. The coupling (112) pairs corruption with abominable iniquity, and the discovery (114) notes it is restated in v3 (alach) - the whole race gone rotten, none doing good. Intensity, specifier and effect are silent (109-111); no prohibition (113). A characteristic (115): moral rot as the consequence-shape of practical atheism - not merely wrong deeds but a spoiled condition of the person.
narratives.story: The fool tells himself there is no God, and the result works its way through everything he is. He does not just do bad things; he becomes rotten, spoiled all the way through. The passage widens this from one fool to the whole human race - looking down from heaven, God finds no one who is good, not even one. Denying God is not shown as a harmless private opinion; it curdles into a corruption that fills the life with abominable wrong. The inner denial and the outward rot are one movement.

narratives.narrative: Here evil is not a lapse but a trade. The sense (101) is paal - to WORK, practise, make - an action (102) whose bearer is the evildoers (105) and whose target is evil, aven (107) - a coupling of verb to object that welds the doing to the thing done. The operation (106) is to work / practise: iniquity as a craft plied. Source (103) is unrecorded; no seat (104: none) fixes it (locus internal:ib-state, 116); manner (108: none) is uncoloured. A second coupling (112) pairs the working of evil with having no knowledge - the discovery (114) sharpening this into a settled practice joined to a wilful ignorance of God. Intensity, specifier and effect are silent (109-111); no prohibition (113). Preserve the distinction from H6466:do (Psa 119:3), where the same verb paal describes doing NO wrong: the identical faculty of doing is here turned to manufacturing iniquity. A characteristic (115): evildoing as vocation, not accident.
narratives.story: The wicked in this psalm do not stumble into wrong now and then; they work at it, the way a person works a trade. Evil is their craft, something they practise and produce. And it goes hand in hand with a chosen blindness - they 'have no knowledge,' not because they cannot know God but because they will not. The same ordinary word for doing and making is used elsewhere for doing no wrong at all; here it is bent to the steady manufacture of harm. Evildoing has become their occupation.

narratives.narrative: The inner life of a whole city is read as its atmosphere. The sense (101) is amal - TROUBLE, toil-mischief, wearying harm - a status (102) filling the city, not a single deed. The bearer is the city's wicked (105); operation (106: none) and target (107: none) are both empty - the reading does not show trouble acting on anyone in the moment; it names a pervading condition. Source (103) is unrecorded; no seat (104: none) fixes it (locus internal:ib-state, 116); manner (108: none) is uncoloured. The one coupling (112) pairs trouble with iniquity - the twin residents that never depart the marketplace. Intensity, specifier and effect are silent (109-111); no prohibition (113). The discovery (114) names it the harmful toil the wicked inflict - wrong that wearies and wounds. Note amal's range across this family (H5999:toil, life's weary labour; H5999:injustic, legalised oppression): here it is civic mischief, wrong soaked into a place. A characteristic (115).
narratives.story: The psalmist looks at his city and sees its whole mood poisoned. Day and night, prowling its walls, are violence and strife; inside, trouble and wrongdoing have settled in like permanent residents, and oppression and fraud never leave the market. This is not one crime but an atmosphere - harm that wearies and wounds, soaked into the streets. The passage does not single out a victim or an act; it names the climate of a place given over to the wicked. The same word can mean honest weariness or legal cruelty; here it is the grinding mischief that fills a corrupt town.

narratives.narrative: This reading is a defence that never gets to happen. The sense (101) is sathar - to HIDE oneself - an action (102) whose bearer is the psalmist (105) and whose operation (106) is to take cover, but only hypothetically: 'then I could hide.' The target (107) is an open adversary - one could conceal oneself FROM a declared enemy. Source (103) is unrecorded; no seat (104: none) fixes it (locus internal:ib-state, 116); manner (108: none) is uncoloured. The coupling (112) pairs hiding with bearing an enemy's taunt - both are refuges an open foe permits. Intensity, specifier and effect are silent (109-111); no prohibition (113). The discovery (114) turns the contrafactual into the wound: hiding is exactly what the betrayal of a friend forecloses, since the traitor was inside the guard. A characteristic (115): the inner reckoning that the deepest injury is the one you cannot take cover from.
narratives.story: The psalmist works out why this betrayal cuts so deep. If an open enemy had insulted him, he could have borne it, or simply kept out of the man's way - you can hide from a foe you can see coming. But this attacker was a close friend, a companion who worshipped beside him. Against that there is no hiding, because the betrayer was already inside his defences. The passage measures the pain precisely by naming the escape that is no longer available: the very intimacy that made the friendship sweet is what leaves him exposed.

narratives.narrative: One of three lexicals in a single verse anatomising a traitor, this names the surface. The sense (101) is chalaq - SMOOTH, slippery, flattering - a status (102) of his speech. The seat (104) is the mouth / speech (inferred); locus internal:ib-state (116). The bearer is the betrayer (105); operation (106: none) and target (107: none) are empty - smoothness is not doing something, it is a quality worn. Source (103) is unrecorded. The manner (108) is 'smooth as butter,' and the coupling (112) sets this surface AGAINST the war hidden in his heart - the reading's whole force is the contrast. Intensity, specifier and effect are silent (109-111); no prohibition (113). The discovery (114) names it the deceptive surface of the traitor, a pleasant exterior masking hostility. Held with its two companions (H7128:war, the heart; H7401:softer, the words), it forms the split between voice and heart that defines treachery. A characteristic (115): the outward oil that conceals the inward blade.
narratives.story: The betrayer's words come out smooth as butter, easy and pleasant to hear. But this smoothness is a surface, deliberately set against what is really inside him. The passage draws the line clearly: the mouth runs smooth while the heart is at war. This is the first of three strokes that together paint the traitor - the smooth speech, the hidden war, the soft words that are really drawn swords. What looks like warmth is a mask. The gap between how he sounds and who he is turns out to be the very definition of treachery.

narratives.narrative: The centre of the traitor triptych: the sense (101) is qerab - WAR, battle, conflict - a status (102), the true content of the man. Its seat (104) is the heart, and the locus (116) is internal:heart - the deepest and most exposing register. The bearer is the betrayer (105); operation (106: none) and target (107: none) are empty, because the finding is not an act but a hidden reality. Source (103) is unrecorded. The manner (108) is 'hidden beneath smooth speech,' and the coupling (112) names it the reality beneath the smooth speech - the same contrast as its companions, now stated from the inside. Intensity, specifier and effect are silent (109-111); no prohibition (113). The discovery (114) calls it the definitive exposure: outward peace, inward war. Distinguished from H2505:smooth (the mouth) and H7401:softer (the words), this is the heart itself - the organ where the enmity actually lives. A characteristic (115).
narratives.story: Beneath all the smooth talk, the passage reaches the man's heart and finds war there. While his mouth pours out friendly, oily words, his inner self is armed for battle. This is the decisive exposure: outwardly all peace, inwardly all hostility. The other two touches - the buttery speech, the words softer than oil - describe the mask; this one names the reality the mask is hiding. War is not something he is about to start; it is what he already is on the inside, in the heart where his real intentions live.

narratives.narrative: The third stroke of the traitor's portrait. The sense (101) is rakak - SOFT, tender, smooth - a status (102) of his words. The seat (104) is the words / speech (inferred); locus internal:ib-state (116). The bearer is the betrayer (105); operation (106: none) and target (107: none) are empty - softness is a quality, not an act. Source (103) is unrecorded. The manner (108) is vivid and self-cancelling: 'softer than oil, yet drawn swords.' The coupling (112) runs parallel to the smooth speech - a second image of the same deceptive surface. Intensity, specifier and effect are silent (109-111); no prohibition (113). The discovery (114) names the paradox: the gentlest speech hiding the sharpest intent, deceit that weaponises tenderness. Preserving the distinction within v21: smooth (the mouth's flattery), war (the heart's reality), softer (the words as concealed blades). A characteristic (115): the tenderest words revealed as edged weapons.
narratives.story: His words are softer than oil - gentle, soothing, disarming. And that is exactly the trap: those same soft words are actually drawn swords. The passage turns tenderness itself into a weapon, so that the kindest-sounding speech carries the sharpest intent. This is the third image in a single verse: buttery speech, a heart full of war, and now words that feel like oil but cut like blades. Softness here is not warmth but disguise - deceit that borrows the sound of gentleness to hide a will to wound.

narratives.narrative: This reading shows the enemy's assault as verbal. The sense (101) is atsab - to INJURE, twist, wrest words - an action (102) whose bearer is the enemies (105) and whose target is the psalmist's words / cause (107). The operation (106) is to injure / wrest - they distort what he says. The manner (108) is 'all day long' (inferred), giving the harassment its relentless duration. Source (103) is unrecorded; no seat (104: none) fixes it. Notably the locus (116) is external:person - this characteristic is realised as one person's aggression against another, not an internal state. The coupling (112) pairs the twisting of his words with their evil thoughts against him - the outward distortion driven by inward malice. Intensity, specifier and effect are silent (109-111); no prohibition (113). The discovery (114) names it the constant twisting of his words, the verbal front of their war on him. A characteristic (115): malice at work through the corruption of another's speech.
narratives.story: The psalmist is under constant attack, and this particular assault is done with words. All day long his enemies take what he says and twist it, wringing his meaning into something they can use against him. Behind the distortion sits their real attitude: every thought they have about him is set on doing harm. This is not a private feeling but an aggression aimed straight at him, person against person - a war fought by bending his words. The twisting outside is powered by the malice inside.

narratives.narrative: Here the inner wrong of rulers becomes a public act. The sense (101) is palas - to WEIGH out, DEAL OUT, mete - an action (102). Its seat (104) is the hands (inferred), and the locus (116) is external:person: the characteristic is executed bodily, in the open. The bearer is the unjust rulers (105); the operation (106) is to deal out / mete, its target violence upon the earth (107). The manner (108) is telling - 'as if weighing it out deliberately' (inferred): a grim parody of the scales of justice, injustice measured out with judicial care. Source (103) is unrecorded, but the previous line supplies it (hearts that devise wrongs); the coupling (112) pairs the dealing-out with the violence itself. Intensity, specifier and effect are silent (109-111); no prohibition (113). The discovery (114) names it the hands executing what the heart devised - inner wrong made outward. A characteristic (115).
narratives.story: The rulers who were supposed to judge fairly do the opposite. In their hearts they plan wrongs, and then their hands carry it out - dealing violence across the land. The chilling detail is how they do it: as if weighing it out on scales, dispensing cruelty with the same deliberate care a judge should give to justice. It is a mockery of the courtroom. What the heart schemes in secret, the hands then measure out in the open, so that the private corruption and the public violence are two ends of one motion.

narratives.narrative: This reading is the bright counterpart to corrupt rule. The sense (101) is din - to JUDGE, govern - an action (102) whose bearer is the king (105). The operation (106) is to judge / govern, its target God's people 'with righteousness' and the poor 'with justice' (107). The manner (108) is 'with righteousness and justice' - the quality that makes the governing good. The locus (116) is external:person: the characteristic is enacted through a ruler's public office. Source (103) is unrecorded, yet v1 supplies it - the justice is God's, given to the king. The coupling (112) names this as the exercise of the king's God-given justice. Intensity, specifier and effect are silent (109-111); no prohibition (113). The discovery (114) marks its defining aim: righteous judgment that takes the side of the poor. Distinguished from its companion H8199:caus (defending the poor's cause), din is the broader act of governing rightly. A characteristic (115): authority used as it was meant to be used.
narratives.story: This is a prayer for a king to rule the way rulers should. Instead of the crooked judges elsewhere in the Psalms, here the request is that the king govern God's people with genuine righteousness and give the poor real justice. The good he does is not his own invention; the psalm asks God to hand him this justice first. And its heart is the vulnerable: righteous government is measured by how it treats the weak and the needy. Where corrupt power crushes the poor, this power exists to judge fairly on their behalf.

narratives.narrative: Paired with din yet distinct, this names advocacy. The sense (101) is shaphat - to DEFEND the cause of, judge for, vindicate - an action (102) whose bearer is the king (105) and whose target is the poor of the people (107). The operation (106) is to defend the cause / vindicate - not merely to rule but to take a side. Manner (108: none) is uncoloured. The locus (116) is external:person: enacted through the royal office. Source (103) is unrecorded. The coupling (112) pairs defending the poor with delivering the needy and crushing the oppressor - a threefold action of rescue. Intensity, specifier and effect are silent (109-111); no prohibition (113). The discovery (114) names the king as champion of the powerless, the heart of the righteous reign. Preserve the distinction from H1777:judg in the same passage: din is governing rightly; shaphat here is the active vindication of the weak - and note how the same shaphat is corrupted in H8199:judg (Psa 82). A characteristic (115).
narratives.story: The prayer for the king goes further than fair rule: it asks him to take the side of the poor. He is to defend their cause, rescue the needy, and crush whoever oppresses them - not standing neutral but actively fighting for the weak. This is the beating heart of a good reign. The very same word for judging is used elsewhere for judges who pervert justice; here it is turned to its true purpose, championing those who have no one else. Real authority, the psalm insists, throws its weight behind the powerless.

narratives.narrative: This is the honest confession of faith nearly lost. The sense (101) is natah - to STUMBLE, turn aside - a status (102) of the believer on the edge. The seat (104) is the feet (inferred), the image of one's standing; the bearer is the psalmist (105); the locus (116) is internal:ib-state. The operation (106) is to almost stumble / nearly slip (inferred), and the manner (108) is 'almost, nearly' (inferred) - the whole finding hangs on that margin. Target (107: none) is empty; source (103) is unrecorded in this row, but the coupling (112) supplies the cause: the near-fall of faith brought on by envy (v3) of the wicked's prosperity. Intensity, specifier and effect are silent (109-111); no prohibition (113). The discovery (114) names it faith on the very edge of collapse - candour about how close he came. A characteristic (115): the inner life admitting its own near-shipwreck, faith not as unbroken serenity but as a footing almost given way.
narratives.story: Asaph makes a startling admission: his faith nearly collapsed. He pictures it as feet almost sliding out from under him, a person about to fall. What pushed him to the brink was envy - watching the arrogant and wicked prosper while he suffered, until he could barely keep his footing. The passage does not pretend to unshakeable calm; it tells the truth about how close he came to going down. Faith here is not a smooth, untroubled thing but a stance that very nearly gave way, honestly named.

narratives.narrative: Looking back on that crisis, the psalmist names its inner taste. The sense (101) is chamets - to be EMBITTERED, soured, to ferment like leaven - a status (102). The seat (104) is the soul; the bearer is the psalmist (105); the locus (116) is internal:ib-state. The operation (106) is to be embittered / grow sour (inferred), with target none (107). The manner (108) is 'pricked in heart' (inferred) - the sharp inward sting that accompanies the souring. Source (103) is unrecorded in this row. The coupling (112) links the bitterness to what it made him: brutish toward God (v22). Intensity, specifier and effect are silent (109-111); no prohibition (113). The discovery (114) names it the soured, resentful state he now confesses. A characteristic (115): bitterness read as a fermentation of the soul that dulls a person into beast-like ignorance - the interior turning sour before it turns back.
narratives.story: The psalmist remembers what his crisis felt like from the inside. His soul had gone sour, fermenting like bread gone bad, with a sharp sting pricking his heart. And he is honest about what that bitterness did to him: it made him stupid and brutish, like an animal in God's presence, unable to think straight about anything. The passage traces the movement from resentment to a kind of dumb, beast-like ignorance. Only afterward, looking back, can he see how the souring inside had blinded him - and how near God stayed the whole time.

narratives.narrative: This reading names the end of the road the psalmist nearly envied. The sense (101) is zanah - to be UNFAITHFUL, play the harlot - a status (102) of those far from God. The bearer is those far from God (105); the operation (106) is to be unfaithful / desert God (inferred), its target 'toward God' (107). The manner (108) is 'far from God, perishing' (inferred) - distance and ruin bound together. The locus (116) is external:god: the characteristic is defined by its relation to God. Source (103) is unrecorded. The coupling (112) sets this faithlessness AGAINST the psalmist's own nearness to God (v28) - the two destinies contrasted. Intensity, specifier and effect are silent (109-111); no prohibition (113). The discovery (114) notes the reversal: their end is the ruin he once envied their prosperity for. A characteristic (115): desertion of God imaged as adultery, and its terminus is destruction - the same zanah appears in H2181:whor (Psa 106) of the nation itself.
narratives.story: After nearly losing his footing over the prosperity of the wicked, the psalmist sees where their road actually ends. Those who live far from God are, in effect, unfaithful to him - like a spouse who deserts the marriage - and that desertion ends in ruin. The passage sets two futures side by side: the faithless, whose distance from God leads to destruction, and the psalmist himself, whose whole good is to draw near. The prosperity he once envied turns out to be a short road to the very end he escapes by staying close.

narratives.narrative: Here the inner life is appetite turned into a claim on God. The sense (101) is shaal - to DEMAND, ask - an action (102) whose bearer is 'they,' the wilderness generation (105). The operation (106) is to demand / ask imperiously, its target food from God (107). Manner (108: none) is uncoloured, but the coupling (112) supplies the setting: paired with the testing heart and the craving - they 'tested God in their heart by demanding the food they craved.' The locus (116) is external:god: the demand is aimed at God himself. Source (103) is unrecorded. Intensity, specifier and effect are silent (109-111); no prohibition (113). The discovery (114) names it the imperious asking born of appetite, a presumptuous claim laid on God. A characteristic (115): craving that dresses itself as entitlement - petition inverted, the creature commanding the Creator, and the passage ties it directly to unbelief (v22, 'they did not believe').
narratives.story: In the desert the people are hungry, and their hunger turns into a demand. Instead of trusting God to provide, they test him, insisting he hand over the food they crave, as though he owed it to them. The passage roots this in the heart: it is craving that has curdled into entitlement, appetite giving orders to God. What should have been humble asking becomes a presumptuous ultimatum. And the psalm connects it straight to their deeper problem - they did not really believe God could or would care for them, so their asking came out as a challenge rather than trust.

narratives.narrative: In God's courtroom the judges' interior is exposed. The sense (101) is avel - INJUSTICE - read here as a disposition (102), a bent of the heart rather than a mere act. The bearer is the judges (105); the operation (106) is to act unjustly, its target 'in verdicts' (107). Manner (108: none) is uncoloured. The locus (116) is internal:ib-state: the reading locates the injustice inside the person, the crookedness behind the corrupt bench. Source (103) is unrecorded; no seat (104: none) fixes it. The coupling (112) pairs the injustice with showing partiality to the wicked. Intensity, specifier and effect are silent (109-111); no prohibition (113). The discovery (114) names it the injustice itself - the crookedness of heart behind the corrupt bench. Distinguished from its companion H8199:judg (the corrupt act of judging), this is the inner disposition that produces it; and note the contrast with H5766:unjust (Psa 43, the enemy's fixed status). A characteristic (115).
narratives.story: God stands up in the divine council and confronts the judges with a blunt question: how long will you keep judging unjustly? This reading looks past the corrupt verdicts to the bent inside the judges themselves - a settled leaning toward injustice, a crookedness of heart. It shows up as favouritism: they tilt the scales toward the wicked. The passage separates the inner slant from the outward act it produces, naming the disposition behind the corrupt courtroom. The problem is not just bad rulings but hearts already crooked before a single verdict is spoken.

narratives.narrative: Paired with the disposition of injustice, this names the corrupt act. The sense (101) is shaphat - to JUDGE, give verdicts - an action (102) whose bearer is the corrupt judges, the 'gods' of the council (105). The operation (106) is to judge / give verdicts, its target 'unjustly' (107) - authority turned against its own purpose. Manner (108: none) is uncoloured. The locus (116) is internal:ib-state. Source (103) is unrecorded; no seat (104: none). The coupling (112) pairs the unjust judging with the injustice and partiality of v2. Intensity, specifier and effect are silent (109-111); no prohibition (113). The discovery (114) names it the corrupt exercise of judgment. The sharp point, preserving the distinction across this family: the very same shaphat is the king's righteous defence of the poor in H8199:caus (Psa 72) - here it is bent the opposite way. Distinguished too from its companion H5766:unjustly, which names the inner bent; this names the perverted act. A characteristic (115).
narratives.story: God's charge against the judges also names what they actually do: they judge unjustly. The office given to protect people is turned against them, so that judging itself becomes a weapon. The striking thing is that this is the very same activity that, in a good king, means defending the poor and rescuing the needy - the identical word, bent to the opposite end. Alongside the crooked disposition of their hearts, the passage names the crooked act it produces: authority using its own power to do the exact reverse of what it exists for.

narratives.narrative: This reading is despair as enclosure. The sense (101) is kala - to be SHUT IN, shut up - a state (102) of the sufferer. The bearer is the psalmist (105); the operation (106) is to be shut in, its target 'without escape' (107). Manner (108: none) is uncoloured. The locus (116) is internal:ib-state - the confinement is felt as an inner condition, not only an outward circumstance. Source (103) is unrecorded, though the surrounding verses supply it (God's wrath, the shunning of friends). No seat (104: none) fixes it. The coupling (112) pairs being shut in with being made 'a horror' to his companions - abandonment and imprisonment together. Intensity, specifier and effect are silent (109-111); no prohibition (113). The discovery (114) names it trapped, walled-in despair with no way out of the affliction. A characteristic (115): the inner being experiencing itself as sealed off - from friends, from relief, from escape - the darkest of the laments where even the cry finds no answer.
narratives.story: This is one of the bleakest voices in the Psalms. The sufferer feels sealed in, walled up with no way out of his misery. His friends have been driven away from him; he has become someone they shudder to look at, and he is left utterly alone. The confinement is not just his circumstances but something he feels pressing in on the inside - a trapped, airless despair. There is no rescue in view, only the feeling of being shut up in the dark. Even so, he keeps crying out, though heaven stays silent.

narratives.narrative: Moses' prayer reads human life itself as weary labour. The sense (101) is amal - TOIL - a state (102). The bearer is 'our life' (105) - the finding is predicated of existence as such, not of one person. The operation (106) is to be full of toil, its target 'and trouble' (107). Manner (108: none) is uncoloured. The locus (116) is internal:ib-state: toil named as the inward texture of the years. Source (103) is unrecorded; no seat (104: none). The coupling (112) pairs toil with trouble - the twin content of even the longest span (seventy or eighty years). Intensity, specifier and effect are silent (109-111); no prohibition (113). The discovery (114) names the wearying labour that fills even the longest life, existence as hard toil soon gone. Note amal's range in this family (H5999:troubl, civic mischief; H5999:injustic, legal oppression): here it is the honest weariness of mortal life under God's wrath. A characteristic (115).
narratives.story: Moses looks at the whole span of a human life - seventy years, or eighty if one is strong - and sums it up with sober honesty: even at its longest, it is mostly toil and trouble, and then it is gone, and we fly away. This is not aimed at one person's hard luck; it is a verdict on existence itself, lived under the shadow of God's anger and the brevity he decrees. Life's inner texture, the passage says, is weariness. The only remedy it looks for is that God would teach us to number our days and give us hearts of wisdom.

narratives.narrative: Against the toil of the previous reading, this is the wise response. The sense (101) is manah - to NUMBER, reckon - an action (102) whose bearer is 'we,' mankind (105), though the psalm frames it as something God must teach ('teach us to number'). The operation (106) is to number / reckon, its target 'our days' (107). Manner (108: none) is uncoloured. The locus (116) is internal:ib-state: counting one's days is an inward discipline. Source (103) is unrecorded. The coupling (112) pairs the numbering with getting a heart of wisdom - the counting is FOR wisdom. Intensity, specifier and effect are silent (109-111); no prohibition (113). The discovery (114) names it the wise reckoning of life's brevity, counting the days so as to spend them well. A characteristic (115): the interior, having faced the weariness and shortness of life (v10), turning that knowledge into wisdom - a numbering that is not despair but the beginning of a wise heart.
narratives.story: Having faced how short and hard life is, the psalm turns that hard truth into a request. It asks God to teach us to count our days - to keep the brevity of life honestly in view. This counting is not meant to crush us with dread; it is meant to make us wise, so that we spend our limited days well instead of squandering them. It is an inner discipline of the heart: hold the shortness of life before you, and it will teach you what actually matters. Facing the end rightly is the start of wisdom.

narratives.narrative: In a single verse the inner being is portrayed as settled trust. The sense (101) is lun - to ABIDE, lodge, spend the night - an action (102) whose bearer is 'the one who dwells with God' (105). The operation (106) is to abide / lodge, its target 'in the shadow of the Almighty' (107). Manner (108: none) is uncoloured. Source (103) is unrecorded - the security is not self-generated but given by the one abided with. The coupling (112) is external:god, and the locus (116) is 'paired with taking refuge' - the abiding is the second half of a pair whose first is dwelling/sheltering in the Most High. Intensity, specifier and effect are silent (109-111); no prohibition (113). The discovery (114) names it the settled dwelling under God's protection - trust as taking up residence with him. A characteristic (115): faith read not as a feeling but as a place one lodges, the interior at rest by staying put in God's shelter.
narratives.story: This single line paints trust as coming home to stay. The person who makes his home in God does not just visit for safety; he lodges there, spending the night in the shelter of the Almighty. The security is not something he manufactures - it belongs to the God he stays with. Trust, here, is less a feeling than an address: you take up residence in God's protection and settle down under his shadow. To abide is simply to keep staying put with him, and that staying is itself the rest and the safety.

narratives.narrative: This reading is the eye of vindication. The sense (101) is nabat - to SEE, behold - an action (102) whose bearer is the psalmist (105). The operation (106) is to see / behold, its target 'the downfall of his enemies' (107). Manner (108: none) is uncoloured. Source (103) is unrecorded. The coupling (112) is internal:ib-state, and the locus (116) is 'paired with hearing their doom' - seeing joined to hearing, a double witness of justice done. Intensity, specifier and effect are silent (109-111); no prohibition (113). The discovery (114) names it the witnessing of God's vindication, the beholding of justice done. Directive 5 (no valence bias): this is satisfaction at the fall of enemies, and the reading reports it plainly - the righteous inner life includes the seeing of judgment. A characteristic (115): the interior looking on as God overturns the wicked, an experience of relief and confirmation grounded not in the psalmist's own act but in what his eyes are given to behold.
narratives.story: On the Sabbath song of praise, the psalmist speaks of watching his enemies fall. His eyes have seen their downfall and his ears have heard their doom - a double witness that God has set things right. This is not squeamish; the passage plainly records the relief of seeing justice done to those who opposed God. He did not bring it about himself; he simply beholds what God has done, and finds in it confirmation that the wicked, however they flourished, come to nothing. Seeing and hearing together, he watches the scales balance.

narratives.narrative: This reading looks without flinching at the wicked's cruelty. The sense (101) is ratsach - to MURDER - an action (102) whose bearer is the wicked (105). The operation (106) is to murder, its target 'the fatherless' (107). Manner (108: none) is uncoloured. Source (103) is unrecorded. The coupling (112) is internal:ib-state, and the locus (116) is 'paired with killing the widow' - the two most defenceless victims joined. Intensity, specifier and effect are silent (109-111); no prohibition (113), though the deed breaks the deepest command. The discovery (114) names it the slaying of the orphan, the wicked's contempt for the helpless. Directive 6 (do not filter): the passage reports the interior of the oppressor as one that will kill precisely those with no protector - widow, sojourner, orphan. A characteristic (115): murder read not as a random act but as the expression of a heart that despises the weak, provoking the psalm's cry for the God of vengeance to arise.
narratives.story: The psalm names the worst of what the wicked do. They kill the widow and the stranger, and they murder the fatherless - deliberately targeting the very people who have no one to defend them. The passage does not look away from this or soften it; it reports the plain horror of an oppressor who preys on the helpless. Behind the killing is contempt: a heart that holds the weak in such disregard it will destroy them. It is exactly this cruelty that makes the psalmist cry out for God, the judge of the earth, to rise up and repay.

narratives.narrative: This reading is the crowded, anxious interior meeting comfort. The sense (101) is sarappim - CARES, anxious thoughts - a state (102). The bearer is the psalmist (105); the operation (106) is to be full of anxious cares, its target 'in the heart' (107). Manner (108: none) is uncoloured. Source (103) is unrecorded. The coupling (112) is internal:ib-state, and the locus (116) is 'paired with God's consolations' - the anxieties set directly opposite the comfort that answers them. Intensity, specifier and effect are silent (109-111); no prohibition (113). The discovery (114) names the crowding anxieties within - the multiplied worries God meets with comfort ('when the cares of my heart are many, your consolations cheer my soul'). A characteristic (115): worry read as a plurality, cares that multiply and press, and the movement of the verse is precisely that God's consolations enter this crowded inner space and gladden it - the anxious heart not scolded but consoled.
narratives.story: The psalmist admits that his worries pile up inside him - not one care but many, crowding his heart at once. But he does not leave it there. In the same breath he says that when those anxieties are at their thickest, God's comfort comes in and cheers his soul. The passage sets the two directly against each other: a heart full of worry, and a God whose consolations answer it. The anxious inner space is real and honestly named, but it is not the last word; into that crowd of cares comes a comfort that gladdens.

narratives.narrative: Here injustice wears the robe of law. The sense (101) is amal - INJUSTICE, mischief - an action (102) whose bearer is 'wicked rulers' (105). The operation (106) is to frame injustice, its target 'by statute' (107) - wrong codified, given legal form. Manner (108: none) is uncoloured. Source (103) is unrecorded. The coupling (112) is internal:ib-state, and the locus (116) is 'paired with the wicked rulers' - the injustice bound to those who legislate it. Intensity, specifier and effect are silent (109-111); no prohibition (113). The discovery (114) names it the manufacture of oppression under colour of law - evil made legal. This is amal's third face in this family (H5999:troubl, civic mischief; H5999:toil, mortal weariness): here it is oppression dressed as legislation. Note the rhetorical point of v20 - such rulers cannot be 'allied with' God. A characteristic (115): wrongdoing that hides inside the machinery of law, the most respectable form of the wicked interior.
narratives.story: The psalm asks a pointed question: can rulers who build injustice into the law itself ever claim God is on their side? These are people who do not break the law to do harm - they write the harm into the statutes, so their oppression looks official and legal. It is wrongdoing wearing a respectable robe. The same word can mean everyday mischief or the honest weariness of life; here it means cruelty manufactured under cover of legislation. The passage flatly denies that God has any part in such a regime - evil is still evil, even when it is legal.

narratives.narrative: This reading is worship as approach. The sense (101) is qadam - to COME, come before, meet - an action (102) whose bearer is the worshippers (105). The operation (106) is to come before God, its target 'with thanksgiving' (107). Manner (108: none) is uncoloured. Source (103) is unrecorded - the impulse is a shared summons ('let us come'). The coupling (112) is external:god, and the locus (116) is 'paired with thanksgiving' - the coming and the thanks inseparable. Intensity, specifier and effect are silent (109-111); no prohibition (113). The discovery (114) names it the drawing near to God, worship as approach. A characteristic (115): the inner life moving toward God, praise framed not as a static feeling but as a directed motion - the whole congregation advancing into God's presence, and doing so thankfully. The reading captures worship's basic grammar: to worship is to come, and to come is to bring thanks.
narratives.story: The psalm opens with an invitation to move toward God: come, let us sing, let us come into his presence. Worship here is pictured as a going-toward - the whole gathering drawing near, advancing into God's presence rather than simply feeling something at a distance. And the approach is never empty-handed; it comes with thanksgiving. The two belong together: to come before God is to come thankfully. It captures the simplest shape of worship - you draw near, and you bring your gratitude with you.

narratives.narrative: This reading is a warning against a movement of the heart. The sense (101) is qashah - to HARDEN, make stubborn - a disposition (102) the people are urged not to adopt. The bearer is the people (105); the operation (106) is to harden, its target 'their hearts' (107). Manner (108: none) is uncoloured. Source (103) is unrecorded. The coupling (112) is internal:ib-state, and the locus (116) is 'paired with the hardened hearts.' Intensity, specifier and effect are silent (109-111). Notably prohibition (113) is present:false, yet the sense itself carries the negative imperative ('do NOT harden') - the prohibition lives in the verb, not in a separate flag; the reading records the warned-against obduracy directly. The discovery (114) names it the heart set against God's voice, the obduracy shown at Meribah and Massah. A characteristic (115): hardening read as something the person does to himself - a self-inflicted deafness to God, held up as the very danger the psalm exists to avert.
narratives.story: The psalm calls its hearers to worship, and then adds an urgent warning: today, if you hear God's voice, do not harden your hearts. Hardening is pictured as something people do to themselves - deliberately stiffening against what God is saying, the way Israel did in the wilderness at Meribah and Massah. It is a self-inflicted deafness. The passage names it precisely because it is avoidable: the alternative to a soft, listening heart is not a neutral one but a hard, closed one. The whole point is to keep that closing from happening today.

narratives.narrative: This reading is affection for a ruined place. The sense (101) is ratsah - to HOLD dear, take pleasure in - a disposition (102) whose bearer is 'the servants of God' (105). The operation (106) is to hold dear, its target 'the stones of Zion' (107). Manner (108: none) is uncoloured. Source (103) is unrecorded. The coupling (112) is internal:ib-state, and the locus (116) is 'paired with pitying her dust' - cherishing the stones joined to pity for the rubble. Intensity, specifier and effect are silent (109-111); no prohibition (113). The discovery (114) names it the love of God's people for Zion, affection even for her rubble. This is ratsah's third face in this family (H7521:approv, endorsing fools' boasts; H7521:pleas, consenting to a thief): here the same faculty of glad approval is rightly placed - fixed on God's city even in ruin. A characteristic (115): love that clings to the very stones and dust of a broken but beloved place, an inner devotion that outlasts destruction.
narratives.story: God's people love Jerusalem so deeply that they treasure even her broken stones and feel tenderness for her very dust. The city lies in ruins, yet their affection does not depend on her being whole; they hold the rubble dear because it is hers. The same inner capacity for delight that others waste on flattering fools or approving thieves is here fixed where it belongs - on God's city, loved even in its brokenness. It is a devotion that outlasts destruction, clinging to the place because of what and whose it is.

narratives.narrative: This reading is idolatry as a ruinous trade. The sense (101) is mur - to EXCHANGE, swap - an action (102) whose bearer is 'the fathers' (105). The operation (106) is to exchange, its target 'the glory of God for an ox-image' (107). Manner (108: none) is uncoloured. Source (103) is unrecorded. The coupling (112) is internal:ib-state, and the locus (116) is 'paired with worshiping the calf.' Intensity, specifier and effect are silent (109-111); no prohibition (113). The discovery (114) names it the fatal swap - the Creator traded for a grass-eating beast. A characteristic (115): the inner act of idolatry read as an exchange, a deliberate substitution in which the infinite glory of God is bartered away for the image of an ox. The passage exposes the absurd arithmetic of the idolatrous heart - it gives up everything worth having for a manufactured animal that itself must eat grass, and the very next line names the result: they forgot their Savior.
narratives.story: At Sinai the people did something staggering: they traded the glory of the living God for a gold statue of a bull. The psalm frames it as an exchange, a swap - and lets the absurdity show. They gave up the God who had rescued them from Egypt in return for the image of an ox, an animal that itself has to graze on grass to stay alive. It is the worst bargain imaginable, everything of worth handed over for nothing. And the moment they made it, they forgot the God who had saved them.

narratives.narrative: This reading is discontent hardened into complaint. The sense (101) is ragan - to MURMUR, grumble - an action (102) whose bearer is 'the fathers' (105). The operation (106) is to murmur / grumble, its target 'in their tents' (107) - grievance nursed in private. Manner (108: none) is uncoloured. Source (103) is unrecorded, though the previous verse supplies it (they despised the pleasant land, having no faith). The coupling (112) is external:god, and the locus (116) is 'paired with not obeying' - murmuring joined to disobedience. Intensity, specifier and effect are silent (109-111); no prohibition (113). The discovery (114) names it the grumbling of the people, discontent turned to complaint against God. A characteristic (115): murmuring read as the voice of unbelief - a discontent that begins in the refusal to trust God's promise and completes itself in muttered complaint and disobedience, the tent-bound grievance that would not obey the Lord's voice.
narratives.story: In the wilderness the people grumble in their tents. It looks small - private muttering behind the tent-flaps - but the psalm treats it seriously. Underneath the complaint is unbelief: they had despised the good land God promised and refused to trust him for it, and the grumbling is what that distrust sounds like. It does not stay mere words either; it goes hand in hand with refusing to obey God's voice. The passage names the whole movement - a discontent rooted in unbelief, voiced as complaint, finished in disobedience.

narratives.narrative: In a single-verse passage the reading confronts idolatry at its most horrific. The sense (101) is zabach - to SACRIFICE - an action (102) whose bearer is 'the fathers' (105). The operation (106) is to sacrifice, its target 'their sons and daughters to the demons' (107). Manner (108: none) is uncoloured. Source (103) is unrecorded. The coupling (112) is internal:ib-state, and the locus (116) is 'paired with pouring out innocent blood.' Intensity, specifier and effect are silent (109-111); no prohibition (113), though the act violates the most basic bond of nature. The discovery (114) names it child-sacrifice, idolatry at its most horrific. Directive 6 (do not filter): the passage reports the interior capable of offering its own children to demons, and the reading does not soften it. A characteristic (115): worship gone utterly monstrous - the same religious act (sacrifice) that should honour God turned into the slaughter of one's own children, the terminus of the idolatrous heart traced across Psalm 106.
narratives.story: The psalm reaches the darkest point of the nation's idolatry: they sacrificed their own sons and daughters to demons. The passage does not flinch or explain it away. The very act of sacrifice, which was meant to honour God, has been twisted into the killing of one's own children, an atrocity that breaks the most natural bond there is. This is where the long slide into idol-worship finally leads - not merely to bowing before statues, but to spilling innocent blood, their children's blood, on the altars of false gods. It is idolatry become monstrous.

narratives.narrative: This reading names the nation's idolatry as adultery. The sense (101) is zanah - to PLAY THE WHORE - an action (102) whose bearer is 'the fathers' (105). The operation (106) is to play the whore, its target 'in their deeds' (107) - the harlotry enacted in what they did. Manner (108: none) is uncoloured. Source (103) is unrecorded. The coupling (112) is internal:ib-state, and the locus (116) is 'paired with becoming unclean' - defilement and harlotry together ('they became unclean by their acts, and played the whore in their deeds'). Intensity, specifier and effect are silent (109-111); no prohibition (113). The discovery (114) names it the spiritual adultery of idolatry - unfaithfulness to God imaged as harlotry. This is zanah's second face in this family (H2181:unfaithful, Psa 73, of individuals far from God): here it is the whole nation. A characteristic (115): covenant betrayal read as sexual infidelity, the interior that whores after other gods and defiles itself in the very deeds that were meant to be worship.
narratives.story: The psalm describes the nation's idol-worship in the language of a betrayed marriage: they played the whore. Turning to other gods was not a neutral change of religion but unfaithfulness to the God they belonged to, like a spouse breaking the marriage bond. And it defiled them - their very deeds, meant to be worship, made them unclean. The image is deliberately shocking: a whole people chasing after other gods the way an adulterer chases other lovers. Behind the statues and the rituals lies a heart that has been unfaithful to the one who loved it.

narratives.narrative: This reading is the body's recoil at the edge of death. The sense (101) is taab - to LOATHE, abhor - a state (102) whose bearer is 'the sick' (105). The operation (106) is to loathe, its target 'all food' (107) - appetite itself has failed. Manner (108: none) is uncoloured. Source (103) is unrecorded, though the passage supplies it (fools suffering for their sinful ways). The coupling (112) is internal:ib-state, and the locus (116) is 'paired with the soul near death.' Intensity, specifier and effect are silent (109-111); no prohibition (113). The discovery (114) names it the revulsion at food of the mortally sick, life recoiling. A characteristic (115): loathing read as the inner sign of dying - the soul so afflicted that it turns from the very food that sustains it, drawing near the gates of death. Note the two loathings in this family: taab here (the sick recoiling from food) against qut in H6962:loath / H6962:disgust (moral revulsion) - the same English word covering bodily collapse and ethical rejection.
narratives.story: Among those the psalm describes are people so sick, brought low by their own foolish ways, that they can no longer stand the sight of food. Their appetite has collapsed; they turn away from the very thing that would keep them alive, and they drift toward death's door. The loathing here is not moral disgust but the body recoiling as life ebbs - the soul near death, unable even to eat. Then they cry out to God in their distress, and he sends his word and heals them, delivering them from the grave they were sliding toward.

narratives.narrative: Uniquely in this family the finding is typed as a faculty (102): the sense (101) is berek - KNEES - a body part standing in for the whole person's collapse. The bearer is the psalmist (105); the operation (106) is to have the knees weak, its target 'from fasting' (107) - grief expressed through the body. Manner (108: none) is uncoloured. Source (103) is unrecorded. The coupling (112) is internal:ib-state, and the locus (116) is 'paired with the gaunt body.' Intensity, specifier and effect are silent (109-111); no prohibition (113). The discovery (114) names it the body failing under grief, strength drained from the very legs. A characteristic (115): the inner suffering read outward onto the frame - the knees, the seat of a person's standing strength, buckling through fasting and sorrow. The interior is not described abstractly but shown in a wasting body: legs too weak to hold the man up, flesh grown gaunt under the weight of scorn and grief.
narratives.story: The psalmist shows his suffering in his own failing body. His knees have gone weak from fasting, his flesh has wasted until he is gaunt and thin. The legs that should hold a person upright can barely support him. This is grief made visible - inner anguish drained down into the body, so that mockery and sorrow leave him physically wasting away. The passage does not describe his pain in the abstract; it points to knees that buckle and a frame gone lean, a man whose whole strength has been poured out by his distress. Out of that weakness he cries to God for help.

narratives.narrative: This reading is generosity as the overflow of a righteous heart. The sense (101) is pazar - to DISTRIBUTE freely, scatter - an action (102) whose bearer is 'the man' who fears the Lord (105). The operation (106) is to distribute freely, its target 'to the poor' (107). Manner (108: none) is uncoloured, but the sense itself carries lavishness (scattering). Source (103) is unrecorded, though the whole psalm supplies it (the God-fearer whose righteousness endures). The coupling (112) is internal:ib-state, and the locus (116) is 'paired with his enduring righteousness.' Intensity, specifier and effect are silent (109-111); no prohibition (113). The discovery (114) names it the lavish generosity of the God-fearer, scattering to the needy. A characteristic (115): giving read as the natural outflow of the fear of the Lord - the same man whose heart is firm and unafraid (v7-8) opens his hand wide to the poor, his generosity so free it is called a scattering, and it is precisely this that his enduring righteousness consists in.
narratives.story: The blessed person in this psalm - the one who fears God and delights in his commands - is marked by open-handed giving. He does not merely share; he scatters, giving freely and generously to the poor. This lavish giving is not a separate virtue tacked on; it is what his lasting goodness actually looks like in practice. The same steady, unafraid heart that trusts God (and so is not shaken by bad news) is the heart that opens wide to the needy. Generosity here flows straight out of reverence for God - a settled character that cannot help but give.

narratives.narrative: This reading is reversal from reproach to joy. The sense (101) is aqar - BARREN WOMAN - a status (102), a condition rather than an act. The bearer is the barren woman (105); the operation (106) is to be given a home, its target 'and made a mother' (107) - a passive receiving, the change worked upon her. Manner (108: none) is uncoloured. Source (103) is unrecorded in this row, though the subject of the whole psalm is God who raises the poor and lifts the needy. The coupling (112) is internal:ib-state, and the locus (116) is 'paired with becoming a joyous mother.' Intensity, specifier and effect are silent (109-111); no prohibition (113). The discovery (114) names it the childless woman, her reproach reversed by God's gift of a household. A characteristic (115): barrenness read as an inner condition of shame that God overturns - the woman does nothing to change her state; she is given a home and made a glad mother, the passage's supreme image of the God who lifts the lowly and reverses their emptiness.
narratives.story: The psalm celebrates a God who lifts the poor from the dust and seats them with princes, and its crowning example is the childless woman. In her world, barrenness carried deep shame and emptiness. But God gives her a home and turns her into a joyful mother surrounded by children. She does nothing to earn this; the change is entirely his gift, worked upon her. Her reproach becomes rejoicing. It is the passage's clearest picture of the God who stoops to the lowly and completely reverses their condition, filling an empty life with gladness.

narratives.narrative: This reading is wonder at a divine reversal. The sense (101) is pala - MARVELLOUS, wonderful - a state (102) whose bearer is the worshippers (105). The operation (106) is to marvel, its target 'at the LORD's doing' (107). Manner (108: none) is uncoloured. Source (103) is unrecorded - the wonder is drawn out by what God has done, not self-produced. The coupling (112) is internal:ib-state, and the locus (116) is 'paired with the LORD's doing' - the amazement inseparable from its object. Intensity, specifier and effect are silent (109-111); no prohibition (113). The discovery (114) names it the wonder of the people at God's reversal, amazement at his work ('this is the LORD's doing; it is marvellous in our eyes'). A characteristic (115): marvelling read as the inner response to God's surprising act - the stone the builders rejected become the cornerstone - an astonishment that spills over into rejoicing and the resolve to make the day one of gladness. Wonder as worship's recognition that God has done the unlikely thing.
narratives.story: Something has happened that no one expected - the rejected stone has become the cornerstone - and the people can only stand amazed. This is the Lord's doing, they say, and it is marvellous in our eyes. Their wonder is not something they worked up; it is drawn straight out of them by what God has done. And it does not stay still: the amazement tips over into rejoicing, and they resolve to make this the day they celebrate and are glad. Wonder here is the heart recognising that God has done the surprising, impossible thing.

narratives.narrative: In the great psalm of the word, this reading is Scripture treasured within. The sense (101) is tsaphan - to STORE UP, treasure, hide away - an action (102) whose bearer is the psalmist (105). The operation (106) is to treasure the word, with target none (107) - the storing is complete in itself, an inward hoarding. Manner (108: none) is uncoloured. Source (103) is unrecorded. The coupling (112) marks it as paired within its char-arc across the psalm, and the locus (116) is internal:ib-state - the heart is the treasury. Intensity, specifier and effect are silent (109-111); no prohibition (113). The discovery (114) names the purpose: 'that I might not sin against you' - the word treasured within as a guard against sin. A characteristic (115): the inner life deliberately laying up God's word inside the heart, an act of storage whose aim is moral protection - not merely knowing the word but hiding it internally so it stands guard over conduct from within.
narratives.story: The psalmist describes a deliberate inner habit: he has stored up God's word deep in his heart, treasuring it away like something precious kept safe. And he tells us why - so that he will not sin against God. The word is not just information he has read; it is laid up inside him where it can act as a guard, steering him away from wrong from the inside out. To keep God's word in the heart, the passage suggests, is to build a defence against sin that goes with you everywhere, quietly shaping how you live.

narratives.narrative: In the same psalm this reading is blamelessness as active innocence. The sense (101) is paal - to DO - here 'do NO wrong,' an action (102) whose bearer is 'the blameless' (105). The operation (106) is to do no wrong, with target none (107). Manner (108: none) is uncoloured. Source (103) is unrecorded. The coupling (112) marks it as paired within its char-arc across the psalm; the locus (116) is internal:ib-state. Intensity, specifier and effect are silent (109-111); no prohibition (113) is flagged, though the negation lives in the sense itself. The discovery (114) names it the blameless who commit no wrong, walking instead in God's ways. A characteristic (115): righteousness read as a doing, not merely an abstaining - the blameless are those who 'do no wrong BUT walk in his ways.' Sharpest of all, preserve the distinction from H6466:work (Psa 53:4), where the identical verb paal names the working of evil: the same capacity to do and make is here turned to committing no wrong and treading God's paths.
narratives.story: At the very start of the great psalm about God's law, the blessed are described as those who do no wrong but walk in God's ways. Notice it is not only about avoiding evil; it is an active thing - keeping to God's paths, living out his law with the whole heart. The very same ordinary word for doing and making is used elsewhere in the Psalms for the wicked who 'work' evil as their trade. Here it is turned the other way: the same energy that some pour into wrongdoing, the blameless pour into doing right.

narratives.narrative: This reading is prompt obedience. The sense (101) is mahah - to DELAY - negated: 'do NOT delay.' It is a disposition (102) whose bearer is the psalmist (105). The operation (106) is to not delay, its target 'God's word' - the commandments he hastens to keep (107). Manner (108: none) is uncoloured. Source (103) is unrecorded. The coupling (112) marks it as paired within its char-arc across the psalm. The locus (116) is external:god - the obedience is oriented toward God. Intensity, specifier and effect are silent (109-111); no prohibition (113) is flagged, the negation carried in the sense. The discovery (114) names it obedience without procrastination ('I hasten and do not delay to keep your commandments'). A characteristic (115): the inner life read as speed toward God's will - not merely willing to obey but refusing to put it off. The finding pairs a positive (hasten) with a negated negative (do not delay), doubly stressing eagerness: when the psalmist turns his feet to God's testimonies, he does it at once.
narratives.story: When the psalmist thinks about his life and where it is heading, he turns straight back toward God's commands - and he does it without dragging his feet. He hastens, he says, and does not delay to keep them. The point is eagerness: not a reluctant, someday obedience, but an immediate one. He puts it in two ways at once - I hurry, and I do not put it off - to underline how ready he is. To love God's word, in this psalm, is to obey it now rather than later, moving toward it without hesitation.

narratives.narrative: This reading is moral revulsion at the faithless. The sense (101) is qut - DISGUST, loathing - a state (102) whose bearer is the psalmist (105). The operation (106) is to be filled with disgust, with target none named in the row (107), though the verse supplies it ('the faithless'). Manner (108: none) is uncoloured. Source (103) is unrecorded. The coupling (112) marks it as paired within its char-arc across the psalm; the locus (116) is internal:ib-state. Intensity, specifier and effect are silent (109-111); no prohibition (113). The discovery (114) names it the revulsion at the faithless, 'because they do not keep your commands.' A characteristic (115): disgust read as the righteous inner recoil from covenant-breakers - not personal spite but a reaction rooted in love for God's law. Preserve the distinction from H6962:loath (Psa 139), the same verb qut but there an even more visceral loathing of God's active enemies; and from H8581:loath (taab), the sick body's recoil from food. Here it is the settled inner disgust of the devout at the faithless.
narratives.story: The psalmist, whose whole heart is bound up with loving God's law, looks at people who break faith with God and feels genuine disgust. It is not petty dislike or personal grudge; his revulsion is aimed at their faithlessness, at the fact that they will not keep God's commands. Because he loves what they despise, their contempt for God turns his stomach. The passage lets this recoil stand as part of a devout inner life - a settled distaste for covenant-breaking that grows directly out of his devotion to the God they are betraying.

narratives.narrative: This reading is joy overflowing at a sudden reversal. The sense (101) is sechoq - LAUGHTER - a state (102) whose bearer is 'the restored people' (105). The operation (106) is to laugh, its target 'at God's reversal' (107). Manner (108: none) is uncoloured. Source (103) is unrecorded - the laughter is drawn out by what God did, not manufactured. The coupling (112) is internal:ib-state, and the locus (116) is 'paired with the shouts of joy' - laughter and shouting together. Intensity, specifier and effect are silent (109-111); no prohibition (113). The discovery (114) names the operation of joy overflowing: the reversal so sudden that the mouth fills with helpless laughter, like waking from a dream. A characteristic (115): gladness read as an involuntary overflow - when God restored the fortunes of Zion, the people were 'like those who dream,' and the joy was so great it spilled out as laughter beyond their control, a delight so full it could not be contained in speech but broke out as laughing.
narratives.story: When God suddenly restored the fortunes of his people, it felt unreal - like waking from a dream. The joy was too big to hold in, and it spilled out as laughter; their mouths filled with it, and their tongues with glad shouting. This is not a polite, measured happiness but an overflow, gladness so sudden and so full that it breaks out on its own. Even the surrounding nations noticed and said, 'The Lord has done great things for them.' The laughter is the sound of a people almost unable to believe their own rescue.

narratives.narrative: This reading is anxiety as the fruit of self-reliance. The sense (101) is etseb - ANXIOUS, painful toil - a state (102) whose bearer is 'the toiler' (105). The operation (106) is to eat the bread of anxious toil, its target 'in self-reliance' (107) - the worry belongs to the one who builds without God. Manner (108: none) is uncoloured. Source (103) is unrecorded, though the psalm names it (building 'unless the Lord'). The coupling (112) is internal:ib-state, and the locus (116) is 'paired with the sleep God gives the beloved.' Intensity, specifier and effect are silent (109-111); no prohibition (113). The discovery (114) names the operation of care: self-reliance turns even bread into anxiety, over against the sleep God gives his beloved without their striving. A characteristic (115): anxious toil read as the interior of the person who labours as if everything depended on himself - rising early, resting late, eating bread soaked in worry - set directly against the restful trust of the one God provides for even in sleep.
narratives.story: The psalm looks at the person who tries to build his life entirely on his own effort - up before dawn, working late into the night, and even then eating bread flavoured with worry. All that striving without trusting God turns ordinary daily bread into a source of anxiety. And the passage sets against it a quiet contrast: God gives sleep to those he loves, providing for them even while they rest. The anxious toil is the inner life of self-reliance; the restful sleep is the inner life of trust. The worry, it suggests, comes from carrying a weight that was never ours alone.

narratives.narrative: This reading is the inner life of harmony. The sense (101) is yashab - to DWELL, sit, remain - here 'dwell in unity,' an action (102) whose bearer is 'brothers' (105). The operation (106) is to dwell together, its target 'in harmony' (107). Manner (108: none) is uncoloured. Source (103) is unrecorded. The coupling (112) is internal:ib-state, and the locus (116) is 'paired with the good and pleasant.' Intensity, specifier and effect are silent (109-111); no prohibition (113). The discovery (114) names the operation itself: brothers living together in concord, the harmony the whole psalm celebrates and images. A characteristic (115): unity read as a shared inner-being state made visible in common life - not a private feeling but a lived-together concord, so good and pleasant that the psalm reaches for images of anointing oil running down and dew falling, and crowns it with God's commanded blessing of life forevermore. The dwelling is the thing praised: relationship as a settled, harmonious abiding.
narratives.story: The psalm opens with an exclamation of delight: how good and pleasant it is when brothers live together in unity.
