The thing being praised is simply people dwelling together in genuine harmony - not a private mood but a shared life lived in concord. It is so good that the psalm reaches for lavish pictures to capture it: precious oil running down the head and beard, dew falling on the mountains. And it ends by saying that this is exactly where God commands his blessing, even life forevermore. Unity among people is treated as something rich, beautiful, and blessed by God himself.

narratives.narrative: This reading is idolatry deadening the idolater. The sense (101) is kemo - to BECOME LIKE - a state (102) whose bearer is 'the idol-makers' (105). The operation (106) is to become like, its target 'the dead idols they make' (107). Manner (108: none) is uncoloured. Source (103) is unrecorded. The coupling (112) is internal:ib-state, and the locus (116) is 'paired with those who trust them.' Intensity, specifier and effect are silent (109-111); no prohibition (113). The discovery (114) names the operation of idolatry deadening its maker: to fashion a lifeless god is to be reduced to its lifelessness. A characteristic (115): a law of the inner life - the idols have mouths that do not speak, eyes that do not see, ears that do not hear, no breath in them; and those who make them, and all who trust them, become like them. Worship shapes the worshipper, so that bowing to the dead makes one dead - the deadness of the object transferred to the soul that reveres it.
narratives.story: The psalm mocks the idols: they have mouths but cannot speak, eyes that cannot see, ears that cannot hear, and no breath at all in them. Then it turns the knife: those who make these lifeless things, and everyone who trusts them, become just like them. There is a law here about the inner life - we come to resemble whatever we worship. Bow down to something dead, and you are made dead inside. The passage warns that idolatry is not harmless; the emptiness of the idol seeps into the person who reveres it, hollowing out the worshipper to match the thing worshipped.

narratives.narrative: This reading is abasement remembered by God's love. The sense (101) is shephel - LOW ESTATE, humiliation - a state (102) whose bearer is 'the people' (105). The operation (106) is to be in low estate, its target 'and remembered by God' (107) - the abasement met by divine memory. Manner (108: none) is uncoloured. Source (103) is unrecorded. The coupling (112) is internal:ib-state, and the locus (116) is 'paired with God's remembering.' Intensity, specifier and effect are silent (109-111); no prohibition (113). The discovery (114) names it the people's abasement, the humbled condition that God's love stooped to remember ('it is he who remembered us in our low estate, for his steadfast love endures forever'). A characteristic (115): the inner condition of a brought-low people read together with the God who does not forget them - the humiliation is real and named, but the whole psalm's refrain answers it, that God remembered them there precisely because his steadfast love endures forever, stooping to a people in the dust.
narratives.story: In its long litany of thanks, the psalm recalls a low point: 'he remembered us in our low estate.' The people had been brought down, humbled, reduced. But the memory is framed by the refrain that runs through the whole psalm - his steadfast love endures forever. Their abasement is named honestly, yet it is not the end of the story, because God did not forget them in it. He stooped to a people in the dust and remembered them, and then rescued them from their foes. Their low place became the very spot where his enduring love reached down to them.

narratives.narrative: This reading is a righteous, visceral loathing - and the passage presents it approvingly. The sense (101) is qut - to LOATHE the rebels - typed here uniquely as an affect (102), a gut-level emotion. The bearer is the psalmist (105); the operation (106) is a visceral loathing that rises against those who rise up against God, its target the loathing itself directed at God's enemies (107). Manner (108: none) is uncoloured. Source (103) is unrecorded. The coupling (112) is 'loathe-rebels' - the affect bound to its object; the locus (116) is internal:ib-state. Intensity (109) is present:false, yet the discovery (114) explicitly notes an intensification: a stronger, gut-level revulsion than hate, 'the body of the affect intensifies.' No prohibition (113). Directive 5/6: this dark-toned affect is offered as devotion ('do I not loathe those who rise up against you?'), immediately followed by the plea 'search me... know my heart' - the psalmist submitting even this loathing to God's scrutiny. Preserve the distinction from H6962:disgust (Psa 119), the same qut but a settled distaste; here it is a fiercer, bodily revulsion. A characteristic (115).
narratives.story: The psalmist asks God a fierce question: do I not hate those who hate you, and loathe those who rise up against you? This is stronger than ordinary dislike - a gut-level revulsion, a loathing that rises up from deep inside against God's declared enemies. And it is offered not as a guilty secret but as evidence of his loyalty to God. Yet in the very next breath he opens himself to examination: search me, God, know my heart, and see if there is any wrong way in me. He holds even this intense loathing up to God, willing to have it tested - devotion and self-scrutiny in the same moment.
